title: Comparative modeling of greenhouse gas emissions from source-separated organics: A case study in New York City.
paragraphs: The waste management sector is the fourth largest source of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the United States (EPA, 2024 ), and globally, waste management emissions are responsible for approximately 5% of global GHG emissions (Gautam & Agrawal, 2020 ; Lambiasi et al., 2024 ). Climate action plans with quantitative GHG goals for cities are on the rise (Cohen et al., 2025 ), and assessing emissions associated with waste management is critical to set GHG emissions reduction goals (Świąder et al., 2025 ). Landfilled waste is often the largest source of GHG emissions for municipalities (Mohareb et al., 2011 ), and in the United States, municipal solid waste (MSW) landfills are the third‐largest source of anthropogenic methane (CH 4 ) emissions (EPA, 2023b ). Landfilling of undigested organic waste is a well‐documented source of CH 4 , which has a 100‐year global warming potential (GWP) 27 times greater than carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) (Pan & Voulvoulis, 2007 ; Themelis & Ulloa, 2006 ). Diverting food waste from landfills is one way to reduce GHG emissions (Yoshida et al., 2012 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The Biosolids Emissions Assessment Model (BEAM) is a spreadsheet tool that models GHG emissions associated with management of organic wastes and is adept at comparing management options (Brown et al., 2010 ). Compared to the EPA's Waste Reduction Model (WARM) (EPA, 2023c ) and IPCC guidance (IPCC, 2006 ), BEAM provides a higher level of granularity and customizability and accommodates a larger volume of real‐world data.

In this study we modeled several management options for New York City's (NYC's) expanding organic waste recycling program in BEAM to determine alternative GHG emissions consequences, assessing GHG emissions associated with five separate management options for source‐separated organics (SSO), which are combined residential food scraps and organics collected from commercial and institutional sources. In an endeavor to meet the city's goals of increasing organic waste collection and reducing GHG emissions by 80% by 2050 (The City of New York, 2016 ), New York City's Department of Environmental Protection (NYC DEP) wanted to reduce GHG emissions associated with the city's public works operations. Accordingly, NYC DEP wanted to understand emissions generated by co‐digestion of SSO (digesting SSO with municipal wastewater treatment solids) and its end products to enable the city to make informed decisions in continuing to pursue their goal of net‐negative GHG emissions from NYC DEP's programs and infrastructure. In support of that goal, this GHG assessment compares four SSO management options that NYC is considering to the historically common method of not separating organic waste from the MSW stream.

The options modeled were based on potential pathways to manage NYC's captured SSO with the goal of comparing the GHG footprints of disposal, composting, and co‐digestion. In a meta‐analysis of life cycle assessments of end‐of‐life management options for organic waste, Morris et al. ( 2013 ) found anaerobic digestion and composting to have lower GHG footprints than other management options, including landfilling and incineration; however, the same cannot be assumed for any given operation due to the influence of feedstocks and site‐specific factors. Where available, BEAM default coefficients were replaced with data from city operations. New York region‐specific climate conditions were used where applicable.

Option 3 : SSO processed by a physical contaminant removal system, made into a slurry, co‐digested in one of the anaerobic digestion systems at NYC's Wastewater Resource Recovery Facility (WRRF), dewatered, and then taken to landfill for disposal.

Option 1 is a baseline scenario to reflect the GHG impact of zero beneficial re‐use of the SSO but is not a pathway that's of interest to NYC. At the time of this research, one pathway for SSO was processing the SSO into a slurry, co‐digesting the slurry at NYC DEP's Newtown Creek WRRF, and using the dewatered digestate for either landfill daily cover or land application. NYC has citywide regulations mandating organic separation and implemented a residential collection program in 2024 (Dougherty, 2026 ). However, most organic waste generated in NYC is currently not separated at the point of generation (is not SSO). NYC has committed to diverting 100% of food waste from landfills (NYC Mayor's Office of Food Policy, 2025 ), and overall, the amount of organic waste diverted from the trash stream has increased since NYC's initial organics diversion efforts in the 1990's (Dougherty, 2026 ). In 2025, the city collected 81,700 Mg of organics out of an estimated total of 1,180,000 Mg of organics entering the waste stream annually (Dougherty, 2026 ). As organics collection programs continue to expand, there is an increasing need to identify the most carbon‐conscious strategies for managing the anticipated increase in SSO volumes.

The data required from NYC DEP to run BEAM for NYC's SSO operation are as follows: SSO characteristics (amount collected and processed annually, nutrient analysis and solids content, physical contamination levels—SSO typically contains measurable levels of glass, metal, plastics, and inorganics that are not compostable nor of value in anaerobic digestion), current disposal practices, composting options available for SSO, NYC's anaerobic digestion processes (energy use, biogas characteristics, amount of biogas generated and flared, fugitive emissions, and biogas to renewable natural gas [RNG] processing steps), and transport distances and means from the SSO collection point to processing and dewatering facilities to the disposal/end‐use site.

BEAM can be customized for a variety of GHG modeling and accounting goals. For this project, GHG accounting began at the transfer station at which SSO are tipped after collections but prior to any processing and ended with the final use or disposal of the material. Figure 1 details the boundaries in which GHG emissions were quantified for each of the five options modeled.

A depiction of the boundaries of the model for each of the five options included in this greenhouse gas (GHG) assessment and the potential GHG costs and benefits captured in each option. The pathways key identifies pathways. The black circles represent emission debits associated with unit processes; white squares represent emission credits associated with unit processes. The transfer station is within the scope of each of the five options. Food waste collection is out of the scope of each of the five options.

Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions are reported in this assessment. In accordance with typical GHG accounting, Scope 1 emissions are direct emissions from management of the modeled biomass; Scope 2 emissions are indirect emissions from purchased electricity or heat; and Scope 3 emissions are indirect emissions from purchased services, production of purchased goods, and transportation (Greenhouse Gas Protocol, 2011 , 2015 ).

One existing pathway for SSO managed by NYC DEP was trucking SSO from the sources to a commercial transfer station in the city, where it was processed into a slurry and transported in tanker trucks to NYC DEP‘s Newtown Creek WRRF. There, the SSO were anaerobically co‐digested with municipal wastewater treatment solids and sent by barge to a dewatering facility. The majority of the dewatered material is used for landfill daily cover with some of the remainder going to land application (The City of New York, 2023 ). Other SSO that was not sent for co‐digestion was composted in‐city or shipped to regional composting and anaerobic digestion facilities (A. Bianco, NYC DEP, personal communication, April 10, 2025).

It is worth noting that the transport from the origin site of the food waste to the transfer station is responsible for some GHG emissions, primarily due to fossil fuel combustion, and those emissions are not accounted for in this study. These SSO‐collection emissions would be the same for each of the five options, and, consequently, they do not impact the comparison of GHG footprints among the five options. Other studies have inventoried emissions associated with collection of food waste (e.g., Madden et al., 2022 ; Matsuda et al., 2012 ; Moult et al., 2018 ).

BEAM inputs were based on data provided by NYC DEP and used in concert with BEAM default values derived from published literature. Alternative options rely on some data‐based estimates that describe viable management alternatives for NYC, as described below. See Table 1 , 2 for a summary of key model assumptions and Supporting Information, Table A1 for a complete list of model inputs.

SSO, both collected by the City of New York Department of Sanitation (DSNY) and from commercial sources, are tipped at a transfer station in Brooklyn, New York. In 2019, the last year before the COVID‐19 pandemic disrupted the program, data from that transfer station indicated that 46,300 Mg (wet weight) of SSO were collected. Of those materials, approximately 44% were collected by DSNY, and the remainder was commercial SSO collected by third‐party haulers. Travel distance, mode of transport, and amount of material going to each site were accounted for in GHG calculations (for all options).

For Option 1 ‐ disposal, the undigested SSO were directed to a mix of disposal options based on DSNY's disposal outlets for MSW at the time of modeling; approximately 69% of the material went to landfills, and approximately 31% went to waste‐to‐energy incineration (combustion) facilities (J. McDonnell, DSNY, personal communication, March 24, 2022).

For landfilling, the capping and gas capture strategies were set to match the “typical” US landfill scenario in WARM. This landfill scenario assumed zero methane capture in the first year after waste is landfilled, 50% capture in years 2–4, 75% capture in years 5–14, and 90% capture after capping in year 15 (EPA, 2023c ). It was assumed that 50% of the methane captured was used to generate electricity and the remainder was flared based on current US landfill gas utilization data (Schauer‐Gimenez et al., 2014 ).

For Option 2 (direct‐to‐compost), it was assumed that the SSO were trucked from the transfer station to a windrow composting operation within 30 miles of the transfer and that the SSO were mixed with leaf and yard waste at a ratio of 1 part SSO to 3 parts leaf and yard waste, by volume, to make the final compost blend. It was also assumed that the windrow composting operation was not using a biofilter cap during composting and that the finished compost was marketed and used an average of 30 miles from the compost facility. In the BEAM, the C:N ratio of the final blend impacts N 2 O emissions, and the lack of a biofilter cap means that CH 4 is released into the atmosphere and not oxidized into CO 2 by a biofilter cap.

For Options 3, 4, and 5, the SSO were modeled to go through depackaging to create a slurry product. Depackaging is a mechanical process to remove inorganic materials (including plastic packaging, glass, metal, and other inert materials) that come in with food waste; the process requires electricity and fuel, which are accounted for in the model. Based on energy tracking by the company managing the depackaging operation (J. Ecker, WM, personal communication, October 24, 2018), the BEAM calculated that the process contributes 0.014 Mg CO 2 eq/wet Mg SSO. As is the case with current management, this slurry was blended with grease trap waste (an additional 10.4% by weight) and transported and fed to the anaerobic digesters at NYC DEP's Newtown Creek WRRF. The physical contaminants separated out from the SSO during depackaging, approximately 7.2% by weight, were directed to a landfill 400 miles by rail from the transfer station (this distance is a weighted average of distances to landfills used by DSNY at the time of modeling) (J. McDonnell, DSNY, personal communication, March 24, 2022; Dougherty, 2026 ) and disposed as MSW. The physical contaminants are predominately inorganic materials that will not generate significant GHG when decomposing in a landfill (Lee et al., 2017 ). See Table 1 for characteristics of the processed slurry.

Using data from NYC DEP (an average of 2,027 data points between 2016 and 2022), a volatile solids (VS) content of 86.5% (dry wt.) was used for the SSO, and based on an estimate from NYC DEP, 75% VS destruction (M. Amar, NYC DEP, personal communication, May 19, 2022) during digestion was used. Based on the initial VS content and the VS destruction, the anaerobic digestion process reduced the mass of the SSO by 65% on a dry weight basis. The amount of biogas generated from the SSO, 0.53 g CH 4 /g VS destroyed, came from a study on the biogas potential of the slurry completed at Bucknell University [1]. For the three options involving anaerobic digestion, it was assumed that all the biogas generated would be cleaned and injected into the natural gas pipeline as RNG in line with current operations at Newtown Creek. The amount of heat and electricity used during the anaerobic digestion process at Newtown Creek was based on typical wastewater anaerobic digestion design (Metcalf & Eddy Inc., 2003 ). The amount of energy needed to run the biogas clean‐up and injection system was included for these options (Options 3, 4, and 5). Energy‐use for biogas clean‐up and injection was provided by NYC DEP. For each of these options, the final digestate was assumed to be dewatered to 35% solids using a relatively energy‐intensive wet air oxidation process (Malcolm Pirnie, Inc., 2005 ), which is currently utilized for dewatering digestate from Newtown Creek.

For Option 3, after dewatering, the digested SSO were directed, now at a much lower mass, to regional landfills. For Option 4, after dewatering, the digested SSO were land applied as Class B biosolids on agricultural land assumed to be a 400‐mile round trip from the dewatering facility by truck. And for Option 5, after dewatering, the digested SSO were modeled to be composted at an aerated static pile composting operation with a biofilter, also a 400‐mile round trip by truck from the dewatering facility, with travel including delivery to the final use site for the compost. As compared to windrows, aerated static pile composting operations typically require less fuel to set up; the biofilter oxidizes CH 4 emissions.

For all five options, the carbon intensity of electricity used in the calculations was 320 g CO 2 eq/kWh, which was calculated from a NYC‐specific electricity inventory (M. Amar, NYC DEP, personal communication, June 17, 2022), which includes a mix of renewable and non‐renewable electricity sources. For context, US EPA's eGRID indicates that the carbon intensity for electricity generation in the 27 subregions of the US range from a low of 125 g CO 2 eq/kWh in Upstate New York (with a high proportion of renewable energy sources) to a high of 726 g CO 2 eq/kWh in Hawaii, which has a high reliance on burning fuel oil to generate electricity (EPA, 2022 ). IPCC AR6 100‐year time frame GWPs were used for calculating the CO 2 eq for non‐fossil methane and nitrous oxide: 27 and 273, respectively (Forster et al., 2021 ). Biogenic carbon dioxide emissions were calculated and reported but not included in the calculated CO 2 eq/dry Mg of biomass managed results, as is standard for biogenic emissions (EPA, 2014 ; IPCC, 2019 ).

Using a carbon sequestration factor of 0.15 CO 2 eq per dry Mg of land‐applied biomass (consistent with Villa and Ryals ( 2021 ) literature review) instead of the default food waste compost carbon sequestration value from the EPA's WARM (EPA, 2023c ).

Using a GWP timeframe of 20 years instead of 100 years. There is an argument for including 20‐year GWPs in GHG assessments due to the urgency of the issue (Abernethy & Jackson, 2022 ), and because activities that emit methane have significantly higher GHG footprints using 20‐year compared to 100‐year GWPs (Cain et al., 2022 ; Forster et al., 2021 ).

Accounting for nitrous oxide emissions from the composted biomass; modeling 0.00055 Mg N 2 O emitted per dry Mg of biomass composted, as calculated from Nordahl et al.’s ( 2023 ) data for emissions from composting the organic fraction of MSW.

Results of the primary analysis (Table 3 ) indicate that composting the SSO then land applying the compost (Option 2), anaerobically digesting the SSO then land applying the de‐watered digestate (Option 4), or anaerobically digesting the SSO then composting the de‐watered digestate and land‐applying the compost (Option 5) have the lowest GHG footprints; the results from these three options are virtually the same. In contrast, landfilling the SSO (Option 1) has the highest GHG footprint. With the assumptions used in the model, digesting the SSO and then disposing of the dewatered SSO in a landfill (Option 3) results in a nearly net‐neutral carbon outcome, which is less favorable than the net‐negative carbon outcomes of Options 2, 4, and 5 but provides for a significantly lower GHG footprint than disposal without anaerobic digestion. Figure 2 shows total GHG emissions associated with the five options for the 50,000 wet short tons (45,372 wet Mg or 5,610 dry Mg; approximately what the city collected annually prior to the COVID‐19 disruption) of modeled SSO, as well as emissions per dry Mg of SSO.

Note : Negative values indicate a net carbon‐negative footprint due to sequestration and/or avoided emissions. Positive values indicate net carbon‐positive footprint (more CO 2 eq of greenhouse gases (GHGs) emitted than sequestered or avoided).

Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with each of the five management options. AD stands for anaerobic digestion. (A) Separated by GHG type and reported in CO 2 eq. The numbers above each bar represent net CO 2 eq per year for each option. In all scenarios, CO 2 emissions are net negative, whereas CH 4 and N 2 O emissions (each represented as a separate component of net emissions) are net positive. (B) Net emissions per dry Mg of source‐separated organic wastes (SSO), as reported in CO 2 eq. The numbers above or below each bar represent the net CO 2 eq per dry Mg SSO for each management.

As is evident in Figure 2 , methane generated during landfilling is responsible for the majority of the GHG footprint in Option 1 (disposal). The SSO have a high VS content and are readily degradable. Consequently, without being digested prior to disposal, placing the SSO in a landfill will induce the transformation of organic carbon to methane (Krause et al., 2023 ). In the first few years after placement in a landfill and prior to capping the landfill, when the conversion of organic carbon to methane (by microbial activity in landfilled waste) is most rapid, a significant amount of that methane can escape to the atmosphere (Krause et al., 2023 ; Oonk, 2012 ; Themelis & Ulloa, 2006 ). As in WARM, BEAM accounts for some carbon sequestration in the landfill scenario; the organic carbon that is not transformed into methane is assumed to be sequestered indefinitely in the landfill. The portion of the disposed SSO going to combustion had minimal impact on the overall GHG footprint for Option 1. See Section 3.3 Note on Combustion‐Related GHGs for Food Waste. The results from this option are similar to the impact that the same biomass would have if it were never diverted from the MSW stream at all, which is common in many cities across the United States (Goldstein et al., 2023 ).

For Option 2 (direct‐to‐compost), the biggest carbon benefit is from carbon sequestration from the finished compost being used as a soil amendment. Another benefit from the composting option is the Scope 3 benefit of adding organic matter‐based nitrogen and phosphorus to soils in the finished compost and consequently eliminating the need for the production of the equivalent amount of synthetic nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers. Manufacturing of synthetic fertilizers produces GHG emissions that may be avoided if organic material is applied instead of fertilizer (Ouikhalfan et al., 2022 ; Roman‐Perez et al., 2021 ; Walling & Vaneeckhaute, 2020 ). Carbon debits in this option come primarily from fuel and electricity used to run the composting operation and methane lost from the piles during composting (the compost operation was modeled without a biofilter cap, meaning less methane oxidation/more methane emissions).

For Option 3, anaerobically digesting the SSO limits the GHG debits associated with landfilling undigested SSO in two significant ways. First, digestion of the SSO, which have a high VS content, reduces the mass of the material by 65% on a dry weight basis, and consequently, much less material is landfilled. Second, because the readily degradable VS have been destroyed during the digestion process, the remaining VS are less readily transformed to methane in a landfill setting (Pan & Voulvoulis, 2007 ). There are still substantive methane emissions estimated to be generated during landfilling, but those emissions are mostly outweighed by the benefits of RNG production, making the overall footprint of this option nearly carbon neutral. The largest benefit from all three of the options that include anaerobic digestion (Options 3, 4, and 5) is the replacement of natural gas with RNG generated during the digestion process.

All transportation‐related emissions for NYC's operations, whether transport by rail or truck (NYC currently uses a mix of these two transportation methods for solid waste disposal), are carbon debits, while other waste management steps can yield credits (e.g., carbon sequestration, replacing natural gas with RNG) or debits (e.g., methane emissions from landfilling, electricity use in dewatering). For the anaerobic digestion Options (3, 4, and 5), there are additional transport emissions associated with trucking the SSO slurry from the transfer station to the digesters and barging the digestate to the dewatering facility in New Jersey. GHG emissions associated with transportation of SSO in the five options modeled are a relatively low percentage of total emissions ranging from 1% (Option 3) to 4% (Option 2) of total GHG emissions, considering both emission debits and credits. A switch to more biodiesel use or electric vehicles with a commensurate growth of renewable energy sources in the grid would lower the overall GHG footprints modeled here; however, the modeling results indicate that transportation is a relatively small portion of the GHG emissions associated with organic waste management.

As SSO collections are expanded to capture a larger percentage of the organics portion of the MSW stream in the future, higher levels of physical contamination are possible (Levis et al., 2010 ). Depackaging is a system for removing a majority of physical contaminants from the SSO waste stream (Catalina Suarez Murcia et al., 2024 ). Electricity and fuel used during the depackaging process is responsible for only 3% of total GHG emissions on an absolute basis for Options 3, 4, and 5. The energy use associated with physical contaminant removal from composting operations is not well documented, consequently GHG costs associated with that process are not included in these calculations.

This modeling project included Scope 3 GHG accounting for the replacement of fertilizers when land applying compost or digestate (avoided emissions) and the production of polymers used in dewatering. For some GHG accounting protocols, Scope 3 emissions are not included (Shrimali, 2021 ). Figure 3 breaks down the total emissions for each SSO management option by scope.

Combustion of biomass in a waste‐to‐energy incineration facility was not one of the options that NYC DEP was interested in pursuing. However, at the time of modeling, 31% of MSW from NYC was going to incinerators. When using BEAM's default values for fluidized bed incinerators and the known solids content of the SSO, BEAM calculates significant GHG emissions, mostly attributed to nitrous oxide emissions produced when combusting nitrogenous wastes (BEAM default values are calculated from Suzuki et al., 2003 ). The EPA's WARM, on the other hand, estimates a net negative GHG footprint largely due to the electricity generated from combusting food waste. WARM assumes 27.8% solids for food waste (unlike in BEAM, the user cannot change this value in WARM), which provides a more favorable balance of British thermal unit value and loss of energy from evaporating water in the SSO during combustion as compared to the 11.2% solids of the SSO modeled in this study. As described by Chen et al. ( 2022 ), moisture and VS content of the material being incinerated have a significant impact on the GHG footprint of incineration, and there are still areas of uncertainty in modeling emissions associated with incineration. For the purposes of this assessment, combustion of SSO (relevant to Option 1) was assumed to be net zero; the GHG benefits of energy captured at the incinerators were assumed to be equal to the GHG debits (nitrous oxide emissions and natural gas use in the combustion process) during combustion of the SSO.

For Option 1 ‐ disposing SSO in a landfill with an aggressive methane capture strategy significantly reduces GHG emissions. Conversely, because methane is the largest contributor to the GHG footprint in this option, when looking at emissions for this option using IPCC AR6 20‐year GWPs (78 and 273 for methane and nitrous oxide, respectively), the GHG footprint more than doubles.

For Option 2 (direct‐to‐compost), using the lower carbon sequestration factor, as opposed to the food waste composting carbon sequestration factor from WARM, emissions associated with composting slightly outweigh benefits associated with carbon sequestration and fertilizer replacement. With this lower carbon sequestration factor, Option 3 is more favorable than Option 2. When modeling nitrous oxide emissions during composting, the GHG footprint increases from −0.55 to −0.4 CO 2 eq/Dry Mg SSO. Additionally, because there are some methane emissions associated with the biological process of composting, when using the 20‐year GWPs the GHG footprint of Option 2 increases but remains carbon‐negative.

For Option 3 – anaerobic digestion to disposal, flaring the biogas instead of cleaning the biogas and injecting RNG into the natural gas pipeline eliminates the renewable energy benefits to the GHG footprint and, consequently, increases overall GHG emissions for this management strategy. As with Option 1, using the 20‐year GWPs significantly increases the GHG footprint, partly due to fugitive methane emitted during flaring of biogas.

For Options 4 and 5 (anaerobically digesting the SSO followed by land application or composting), most of the sensitivity adjustments have minimal impact on GHG emissions. However, when flaring the biogas instead of injecting RNG into the pipeline, both of these options become slightly carbon‐positive. And when modeling nitrous oxide emissions from composting, the GHG footprint of Option 5 changes from −0.59 to −0.44 CO 2 eq/Dry Mg SSO.

The results from both the primary analysis and the sensitivity analyses make it clear that, unless biogas is flared instead of used for RNG, Options 4 and 5 (anaerobic digestion followed by land application or composting then land application, respectively, of the dewatered digestate) offer the most favorable GHG outcome.

The favorability of Option 2, direct‐to‐compost, including land application of the compost, is highly dependent on the carbon sequestration factor, more so than for Options 4 (anaerobic digestion to land‐application) and 5 (anaerobic digestion to compost), where the benefits of RNG to pipeline persist regardless of the carbon sequestration factor. The permanence of soil carbon introduced by organic soil amendments is both difficult to measure and highly variable. There is currently little consensus on what value to use, with published estimates ranging from 0.013 MgCO 2 eq/dry Mg biomass (Villa & Ryals, 2021 ) to 0.98 MgCO 2 eq/dry Mg biomass (EPA, 2023a ) and an array of values in between (e.g., Coleman & Jenkinson, 1996 ; Levavasseur et al., 2020 ; Parton et al., 1993 ). This highlights a need for further research on long‐term soil carbon storage and the development of a standardized framework for soil organic carbon measurement and monitoring (Lawrence et al., 2023 ).

Option 3 (anaerobic digestion to disposal) still provides for a low GHG footprint, though significantly less favorable than Options 2, 4, and 5. The exceptions are if modeled with 20‐year GWPs or if biogas is flared instead of used for RNG; in these cases, the GHG footprint is net positive.

Option 1 (disposal) remains the least favorable option in all sensitivity analyses. However, for any waste that is landfilled, this modeling effort indicates that municipalities focused on reducing emissions should focus on selecting landfills with aggressive capping and gas capture strategies is an option for reducing emissions.

When comparing the management options of diverting SSO directly to composting versus diverting the material to anaerobic digestion followed by land application or composting, there are material management considerations to consider. The SSO collected at the NYC transfer station has a low solids content, partly due to blending commercial organic waste streams with food waste streams. With the physical contamination that is expected with large‐scale SSO diversion programs (Thakali et al., 2022 ), the use of depackaging equipment to remove physical contamination results in a slurry; this high‐moisture slurry would likely be problematic for composting. With a diverse recycling program in the future, NYC may find that some SSO feedstocks are more suitable for anaerobic digestion, while some less physically contaminated, higher solids SSO may be better suited to going directly to composting.

In weighing Option 4 versus Option 5, the two options with the most similar and most favorable GHG outcomes, there are two important considerations. First is that compost is a more versatile soil amendment than dewatered digestate. Compost may be used in landscaping, gardens, and agricultural fields, whereas dewatered digestate is a moist, sometimes odoriferous material that often contains more nitrogen than compost (on a mass basis) and is best suited for use in agricultural fields rather than landscaping and gardens. Second is that composting and then land‐applying the dewatered digestate is a more labor‐intensive and costly process than simply land‐applying the dewatered digestate. In either case, NYC would likely be exporting the material to a third party to handle composting and/or land application.

Lastly, the options modeled in this GHG assessment are based on practical options available for NYC's SSO at the time of this study. It is worth noting that there are other options for waste management, including pyrolysis and combustion of SSO and/or dewatered digestate, that were not modeled in this study and may be worth considering for other waste management entities (e.g., Havukainen et al., 2022 ).

Although there is no exact comparison to this analysis in the literature due to the specifications of this SSO and the management options, other analyses have reported similar outcomes when comparing emissions from landfilling, anaerobic digestion, and composting of organic waste. Nordahl et al. ( 2020 ) found that landfilling organic waste had a significantly higher GHG footprint than composting or digesting, and composting and land‐applying the digestate rather than landfilling the digestate improved the GHG footprint. In a review of 19 studies on GHG emissions associated with food waste management, Bernstad Saraiva Schott et al. ( 2016 ) found that, when energy is recovered during digestion, anaerobic digestion is often preferable to composting (as well as to landfilling and incineration). These studies offer better comparisons for Options 1, 2, and 4 than for the other scenarios. In units of Mg CO 2 e per wet Mg of organic waste, the results from this study are 0.24 for Option 1 (landfill), −0.062 for Option 2 (direct to compost), and −0.065 for Option 4 (anaerobic digestion to land application). Findings from Nordahl et al. ( 2020 ), Bernstad Saraiva Schott et al. ( 2016 ), and Morris et al. ( 2013 ) for similar management scenarios range from 0.16 to 0.50 Mg CO 2 e per wet Mg of organic waste for landfilling, −0.21 to 0.14 for composting, and −0.39 to 0.027 for anaerobic digestion; these ranges encompass the results from this study.

Using BEAM, we achieved a high level of granularity specific to GHG emissions associated with current waste management data and diversion options that were available to NYC at the time of this study. The accompanying sensitivity analyses highlight the model's responsiveness to the values to which the model is most sensitive and to values that are most likely to change in the rapidly evolving field of GHG accounting. This assessment found that, of the SSO management options available to NYC, anaerobic digestion followed by land application of the digestate (composted or not) offered the most favorable GHG footprint, followed closely by composting without anaerobic digestion. The sensitivity analyses found that flaring the biogas from anaerobic digestion, instead of recycling it into RNG, increased the GHG footprint of the three anaerobic digestion options (Options 3, 4, and 5) and changed Options 4 and 5 from net‐negative to net‐positive (significantly less favorable). Similarly, using a lower carbon sequestration factor changed the GHG footprint of Option 2 (direct‐to‐compost) from net‐negative to net‐positive. In all the sensitivity analyses in this assessment, landfilling undigested SSO remained the least‐favorable option from a GHG perspective. As such, BEAM served as an evidence‐based decision‐support tool for NYC DEP while modeling the significant impact management decision alternatives can have on the emissions associated with organic waste management. Factors that are rapidly changing in today's waste management marketplace, including landfill management strategies and RNG use, can have dramatic impacts on emissions associated with organic waste management. The sensitivity analysis of the impact of the carbon sequestration factor utilized highlights the need for further research and consensus in GHG accounting methodologies with particular attention to the carbon sequestration factor used to calculate the permanence of carbon in land‐applied biomass. This modeling would not be possible in WARM, where there are limited options for customizing model inputs; WARM values that are not adjustable by the user include biogas collection rate, methane flare rate, fugitive emissions from digesters, solids content of organic wastes, and composting parameters such as presence of a biofilter and rate of nitrous oxide emissions. WARM also does not allow for the combination of processing options, such as digestion followed by composting or land application. Working with BEAM was essential to customizing the modeling to NYC's operations and to understanding the impact of potential management changes. Projecting increased diversion of SSO, the NYC DEP plans to expand SSO collections directed to anaerobic digestion to approximately 300,000 Mg/year by 2035. (A. Bianco, NYC DEP, personal communication, December 30, 2025). Based on the estimates from this modeling, if this material were to be managed in accordance with Option 5, the city would reduce GHG emissions by 102,005 Mg CO 2 eq/year compared to not separating that organic waste from the MSW stream.

Andrew Carpenter : Conceptualization; formal analysis; investigation; methodology; project administration; writing—original draft; writing—review and editing. Romy Carpenter : Data curation; visualization; writing—original draft; writing—review and editing. Ivan J Fernandez : Writing—review and editing.

Carpenter, A. , Carpenter, R. , & Fernandez, I. (2026). Comparative modeling of greenhouse gas emissions from source‐separated organics: A case study in New York City. Journal of Environmental Quality, 55, e70227. 10.1002/jeq2.70227

The waste management sector is the fourth largest source of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the United States (EPA, 2024 ), and globally, waste management emissions are responsible for approximately 5% of global GHG emissions (Gautam & Agrawal, 2020 ; Lambiasi et al., 2024 ). Climate action plans with quantitative GHG goals for cities are on the rise (Cohen et al., 2025 ), and assessing emissions associated with waste management is critical to set GHG emissions reduction goals (Świąder et al., 2025 ). Landfilled waste is often the largest source of GHG emissions for municipalities (Mohareb et al., 2011 ), and in the United States, municipal solid waste (MSW) landfills are the third‐largest source of anthropogenic methane (CH 4 ) emissions (EPA, 2023b ). Landfilling of undigested organic waste is a well‐documented source of CH 4 , which has a 100‐year global warming potential (GWP) 27 times greater than carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) (Pan & Voulvoulis, 2007 ; Themelis & Ulloa, 2006 ). Diverting food waste from landfills is one way to reduce GHG emissions (Yoshida et al., 2012 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The Biosolids Emissions Assessment Model (BEAM) is a spreadsheet tool that models GHG emissions associated with management of organic wastes and is adept at comparing management options (Brown et al., 2010 ). Compared to the EPA's Waste Reduction Model (WARM) (EPA, 2023c ) and IPCC guidance (IPCC, 2006 ), BEAM provides a higher level of granularity and customizability and accommodates a larger volume of real‐world data.

In this study we modeled several management options for New York City's (NYC's) expanding organic waste recycling program in BEAM to determine alternative GHG emissions consequences, assessing GHG emissions associated with five separate management options for source‐separated organics (SSO), which are combined residential food scraps and organics collected from commercial and institutional sources. In an endeavor to meet the city's goals of increasing organic waste collection and reducing GHG emissions by 80% by 2050 (The City of New York, 2016 ), New York City's Department of Environmental Protection (NYC DEP) wanted to reduce GHG emissions associated with the city's public works operations. Accordingly, NYC DEP wanted to understand emissions generated by co‐digestion of SSO (digesting SSO with municipal wastewater treatment solids) and its end products to enable the city to make informed decisions in continuing to pursue their goal of net‐negative GHG emissions from NYC DEP's programs and infrastructure. In support of that goal, this GHG assessment compares four SSO management options that NYC is considering to the historically common method of not separating organic waste from the MSW stream.

The options modeled were based on potential pathways to manage NYC's captured SSO with the goal of comparing the GHG footprints of disposal, composting, and co‐digestion. In a meta‐analysis of life cycle assessments of end‐of‐life management options for organic waste, Morris et al. ( 2013 ) found anaerobic digestion and composting to have lower GHG footprints than other management options, including landfilling and incineration; however, the same cannot be assumed for any given operation due to the influence of feedstocks and site‐specific factors. Where available, BEAM default coefficients were replaced with data from city operations. New York region‐specific climate conditions were used where applicable.

Option 3 : SSO processed by a physical contaminant removal system, made into a slurry, co‐digested in one of the anaerobic digestion systems at NYC's Wastewater Resource Recovery Facility (WRRF), dewatered, and then taken to landfill for disposal.

Option 1 is a baseline scenario to reflect the GHG impact of zero beneficial re‐use of the SSO but is not a pathway that's of interest to NYC. At the time of this research, one pathway for SSO was processing the SSO into a slurry, co‐digesting the slurry at NYC DEP's Newtown Creek WRRF, and using the dewatered digestate for either landfill daily cover or land application. NYC has citywide regulations mandating organic separation and implemented a residential collection program in 2024 (Dougherty, 2026 ). However, most organic waste generated in NYC is currently not separated at the point of generation (is not SSO). NYC has committed to diverting 100% of food waste from landfills (NYC Mayor's Office of Food Policy, 2025 ), and overall, the amount of organic waste diverted from the trash stream has increased since NYC's initial organics diversion efforts in the 1990's (Dougherty, 2026 ). In 2025, the city collected 81,700 Mg of organics out of an estimated total of 1,180,000 Mg of organics entering the waste stream annually (Dougherty, 2026 ). As organics collection programs continue to expand, there is an increasing need to identify the most carbon‐conscious strategies for managing the anticipated increase in SSO volumes.

The data required from NYC DEP to run BEAM for NYC's SSO operation are as follows: SSO characteristics (amount collected and processed annually, nutrient analysis and solids content, physical contamination levels—SSO typically contains measurable levels of glass, metal, plastics, and inorganics that are not compostable nor of value in anaerobic digestion), current disposal practices, composting options available for SSO, NYC's anaerobic digestion processes (energy use, biogas characteristics, amount of biogas generated and flared, fugitive emissions, and biogas to renewable natural gas [RNG] processing steps), and transport distances and means from the SSO collection point to processing and dewatering facilities to the disposal/end‐use site.

BEAM can be customized for a variety of GHG modeling and accounting goals. For this project, GHG accounting began at the transfer station at which SSO are tipped after collections but prior to any processing and ended with the final use or disposal of the material. Figure 1 details the boundaries in which GHG emissions were quantified for each of the five options modeled.

A depiction of the boundaries of the model for each of the five options included in this greenhouse gas (GHG) assessment and the potential GHG costs and benefits captured in each option. The pathways key identifies pathways. The black circles represent emission debits associated with unit processes; white squares represent emission credits associated with unit processes. The transfer station is within the scope of each of the five options. Food waste collection is out of the scope of each of the five options.

Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions are reported in this assessment. In accordance with typical GHG accounting, Scope 1 emissions are direct emissions from management of the modeled biomass; Scope 2 emissions are indirect emissions from purchased electricity or heat; and Scope 3 emissions are indirect emissions from purchased services, production of purchased goods, and transportation (Greenhouse Gas Protocol, 2011 , 2015 ).

One existing pathway for SSO managed by NYC DEP was trucking SSO from the sources to a commercial transfer station in the city, where it was processed into a slurry and transported in tanker trucks to NYC DEP‘s Newtown Creek WRRF. There, the SSO were anaerobically co‐digested with municipal wastewater treatment solids and sent by barge to a dewatering facility. The majority of the dewatered material is used for landfill daily cover with some of the remainder going to land application (The City of New York, 2023 ). Other SSO that was not sent for co‐digestion was composted in‐city or shipped to regional composting and anaerobic digestion facilities (A. Bianco, NYC DEP, personal communication, April 10, 2025).

It is worth noting that the transport from the origin site of the food waste to the transfer station is responsible for some GHG emissions, primarily due to fossil fuel combustion, and those emissions are not accounted for in this study. These SSO‐collection emissions would be the same for each of the five options, and, consequently, they do not impact the comparison of GHG footprints among the five options. Other studies have inventoried emissions associated with collection of food waste (e.g., Madden et al., 2022 ; Matsuda et al., 2012 ; Moult et al., 2018 ).

BEAM inputs were based on data provided by NYC DEP and used in concert with BEAM default values derived from published literature. Alternative options rely on some data‐based estimates that describe viable management alternatives for NYC, as described below. See Table 1 , 2 for a summary of key model assumptions and Supporting Information, Table A1 for a complete list of model inputs.

SSO, both collected by the City of New York Department of Sanitation (DSNY) and from commercial sources, are tipped at a transfer station in Brooklyn, New York. In 2019, the last year before the COVID‐19 pandemic disrupted the program, data from that transfer station indicated that 46,300 Mg (wet weight) of SSO were collected. Of those materials, approximately 44% were collected by DSNY, and the remainder was commercial SSO collected by third‐party haulers. Travel distance, mode of transport, and amount of material going to each site were accounted for in GHG calculations (for all options).

For Option 1 ‐ disposal, the undigested SSO were directed to a mix of disposal options based on DSNY's disposal outlets for MSW at the time of modeling; approximately 69% of the material went to landfills, and approximately 31% went to waste‐to‐energy incineration (combustion) facilities (J. McDonnell, DSNY, personal communication, March 24, 2022).

For landfilling, the capping and gas capture strategies were set to match the “typical” US landfill scenario in WARM. This landfill scenario assumed zero methane capture in the first year after waste is landfilled, 50% capture in years 2–4, 75% capture in years 5–14, and 90% capture after capping in year 15 (EPA, 2023c ). It was assumed that 50% of the methane captured was used to generate electricity and the remainder was flared based on current US landfill gas utilization data (Schauer‐Gimenez et al., 2014 ).

For Option 2 (direct‐to‐compost), it was assumed that the SSO were trucked from the transfer station to a windrow composting operation within 30 miles of the transfer and that the SSO were mixed with leaf and yard waste at a ratio of 1 part SSO to 3 parts leaf and yard waste, by volume, to make the final compost blend. It was also assumed that the windrow composting operation was not using a biofilter cap during composting and that the finished compost was marketed and used an average of 30 miles from the compost facility. In the BEAM, the C:N ratio of the final blend impacts N 2 O emissions, and the lack of a biofilter cap means that CH 4 is released into the atmosphere and not oxidized into CO 2 by a biofilter cap.

For Options 3, 4, and 5, the SSO were modeled to go through depackaging to create a slurry product. Depackaging is a mechanical process to remove inorganic materials (including plastic packaging, glass, metal, and other inert materials) that come in with food waste; the process requires electricity and fuel, which are accounted for in the model. Based on energy tracking by the company managing the depackaging operation (J. Ecker, WM, personal communication, October 24, 2018), the BEAM calculated that the process contributes 0.014 Mg CO 2 eq/wet Mg SSO. As is the case with current management, this slurry was blended with grease trap waste (an additional 10.4% by weight) and transported and fed to the anaerobic digesters at NYC DEP's Newtown Creek WRRF. The physical contaminants separated out from the SSO during depackaging, approximately 7.2% by weight, were directed to a landfill 400 miles by rail from the transfer station (this distance is a weighted average of distances to landfills used by DSNY at the time of modeling) (J. McDonnell, DSNY, personal communication, March 24, 2022; Dougherty, 2026 ) and disposed as MSW. The physical contaminants are predominately inorganic materials that will not generate significant GHG when decomposing in a landfill (Lee et al., 2017 ). See Table 1 for characteristics of the processed slurry.

Using data from NYC DEP (an average of 2,027 data points between 2016 and 2022), a volatile solids (VS) content of 86.5% (dry wt.) was used for the SSO, and based on an estimate from NYC DEP, 75% VS destruction (M. Amar, NYC DEP, personal communication, May 19, 2022) during digestion was used. Based on the initial VS content and the VS destruction, the anaerobic digestion process reduced the mass of the SSO by 65% on a dry weight basis. The amount of biogas generated from the SSO, 0.53 g CH 4 /g VS destroyed, came from a study on the biogas potential of the slurry completed at Bucknell University [1]. For the three options involving anaerobic digestion, it was assumed that all the biogas generated would be cleaned and injected into the natural gas pipeline as RNG in line with current operations at Newtown Creek. The amount of heat and electricity used during the anaerobic digestion process at Newtown Creek was based on typical wastewater anaerobic digestion design (Metcalf & Eddy Inc., 2003 ). The amount of energy needed to run the biogas clean‐up and injection system was included for these options (Options 3, 4, and 5). Energy‐use for biogas clean‐up and injection was provided by NYC DEP. For each of these options, the final digestate was assumed to be dewatered to 35% solids using a relatively energy‐intensive wet air oxidation process (Malcolm Pirnie, Inc., 2005 ), which is currently utilized for dewatering digestate from Newtown Creek.

For Option 3, after dewatering, the digested SSO were directed, now at a much lower mass, to regional landfills. For Option 4, after dewatering, the digested SSO were land applied as Class B biosolids on agricultural land assumed to be a 400‐mile round trip from the dewatering facility by truck. And for Option 5, after dewatering, the digested SSO were modeled to be composted at an aerated static pile composting operation with a biofilter, also a 400‐mile round trip by truck from the dewatering facility, with travel including delivery to the final use site for the compost. As compared to windrows, aerated static pile composting operations typically require less fuel to set up; the biofilter oxidizes CH 4 emissions.

For all five options, the carbon intensity of electricity used in the calculations was 320 g CO 2 eq/kWh, which was calculated from a NYC‐specific electricity inventory (M. Amar, NYC DEP, personal communication, June 17, 2022), which includes a mix of renewable and non‐renewable electricity sources. For context, US EPA's eGRID indicates that the carbon intensity for electricity generation in the 27 subregions of the US range from a low of 125 g CO 2 eq/kWh in Upstate New York (with a high proportion of renewable energy sources) to a high of 726 g CO 2 eq/kWh in Hawaii, which has a high reliance on burning fuel oil to generate electricity (EPA, 2022 ). IPCC AR6 100‐year time frame GWPs were used for calculating the CO 2 eq for non‐fossil methane and nitrous oxide: 27 and 273, respectively (Forster et al., 2021 ). Biogenic carbon dioxide emissions were calculated and reported but not included in the calculated CO 2 eq/dry Mg of biomass managed results, as is standard for biogenic emissions (EPA, 2014 ; IPCC, 2019 ).

Using a carbon sequestration factor of 0.15 CO 2 eq per dry Mg of land‐applied biomass (consistent with Villa and Ryals ( 2021 ) literature review) instead of the default food waste compost carbon sequestration value from the EPA's WARM (EPA, 2023c ).

Using a GWP timeframe of 20 years instead of 100 years. There is an argument for including 20‐year GWPs in GHG assessments due to the urgency of the issue (Abernethy & Jackson, 2022 ), and because activities that emit methane have significantly higher GHG footprints using 20‐year compared to 100‐year GWPs (Cain et al., 2022 ; Forster et al., 2021 ).

Accounting for nitrous oxide emissions from the composted biomass; modeling 0.00055 Mg N 2 O emitted per dry Mg of biomass composted, as calculated from Nordahl et al.’s ( 2023 ) data for emissions from composting the organic fraction of MSW.

Results of the primary analysis (Table 3 ) indicate that composting the SSO then land applying the compost (Option 2), anaerobically digesting the SSO then land applying the de‐watered digestate (Option 4), or anaerobically digesting the SSO then composting the de‐watered digestate and land‐applying the compost (Option 5) have the lowest GHG footprints; the results from these three options are virtually the same. In contrast, landfilling the SSO (Option 1) has the highest GHG footprint. With the assumptions used in the model, digesting the SSO and then disposing of the dewatered SSO in a landfill (Option 3) results in a nearly net‐neutral carbon outcome, which is less favorable than the net‐negative carbon outcomes of Options 2, 4, and 5 but provides for a significantly lower GHG footprint than disposal without anaerobic digestion. Figure 2 shows total GHG emissions associated with the five options for the 50,000 wet short tons (45,372 wet Mg or 5,610 dry Mg; approximately what the city collected annually prior to the COVID‐19 disruption) of modeled SSO, as well as emissions per dry Mg of SSO.

Note : Negative values indicate a net carbon‐negative footprint due to sequestration and/or avoided emissions. Positive values indicate net carbon‐positive footprint (more CO 2 eq of greenhouse gases (GHGs) emitted than sequestered or avoided).

Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with each of the five management options. AD stands for anaerobic digestion. (A) Separated by GHG type and reported in CO 2 eq. The numbers above each bar represent net CO 2 eq per year for each option. In all scenarios, CO 2 emissions are net negative, whereas CH 4 and N 2 O emissions (each represented as a separate component of net emissions) are net positive. (B) Net emissions per dry Mg of source‐separated organic wastes (SSO), as reported in CO 2 eq. The numbers above or below each bar represent the net CO 2 eq per dry Mg SSO for each management.

As is evident in Figure 2 , methane generated during landfilling is responsible for the majority of the GHG footprint in Option 1 (disposal). The SSO have a high VS content and are readily degradable. Consequently, without being digested prior to disposal, placing the SSO in a landfill will induce the transformation of organic carbon to methane (Krause et al., 2023 ). In the first few years after placement in a landfill and prior to capping the landfill, when the conversion of organic carbon to methane (by microbial activity in landfilled waste) is most rapid, a significant amount of that methane can escape to the atmosphere (Krause et al., 2023 ; Oonk, 2012 ; Themelis & Ulloa, 2006 ). As in WARM, BEAM accounts for some carbon sequestration in the landfill scenario; the organic carbon that is not transformed into methane is assumed to be sequestered indefinitely in the landfill. The portion of the disposed SSO going to combustion had minimal impact on the overall GHG footprint for Option 1. See Section 3.3 Note on Combustion‐Related GHGs for Food Waste. The results from this option are similar to the impact that the same biomass would have if it were never diverted from the MSW stream at all, which is common in many cities across the United States (Goldstein et al., 2023 ).

For Option 2 (direct‐to‐compost), the biggest carbon benefit is from carbon sequestration from the finished compost being used as a soil amendment. Another benefit from the composting option is the Scope 3 benefit of adding organic matter‐based nitrogen and phosphorus to soils in the finished compost and consequently eliminating the need for the production of the equivalent amount of synthetic nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers. Manufacturing of synthetic fertilizers produces GHG emissions that may be avoided if organic material is applied instead of fertilizer (Ouikhalfan et al., 2022 ; Roman‐Perez et al., 2021 ; Walling & Vaneeckhaute, 2020 ). Carbon debits in this option come primarily from fuel and electricity used to run the composting operation and methane lost from the piles during composting (the compost operation was modeled without a biofilter cap, meaning less methane oxidation/more methane emissions).

For Option 3, anaerobically digesting the SSO limits the GHG debits associated with landfilling undigested SSO in two significant ways. First, digestion of the SSO, which have a high VS content, reduces the mass of the material by 65% on a dry weight basis, and consequently, much less material is landfilled. Second, because the readily degradable VS have been destroyed during the digestion process, the remaining VS are less readily transformed to methane in a landfill setting (Pan & Voulvoulis, 2007 ). There are still substantive methane emissions estimated to be generated during landfilling, but those emissions are mostly outweighed by the benefits of RNG production, making the overall footprint of this option nearly carbon neutral. The largest benefit from all three of the options that include anaerobic digestion (Options 3, 4, and 5) is the replacement of natural gas with RNG generated during the digestion process.

All transportation‐related emissions for NYC's operations, whether transport by rail or truck (NYC currently uses a mix of these two transportation methods for solid waste disposal), are carbon debits, while other waste management steps can yield credits (e.g., carbon sequestration, replacing natural gas with RNG) or debits (e.g., methane emissions from landfilling, electricity use in dewatering). For the anaerobic digestion Options (3, 4, and 5), there are additional transport emissions associated with trucking the SSO slurry from the transfer station to the digesters and barging the digestate to the dewatering facility in New Jersey. GHG emissions associated with transportation of SSO in the five options modeled are a relatively low percentage of total emissions ranging from 1% (Option 3) to 4% (Option 2) of total GHG emissions, considering both emission debits and credits. A switch to more biodiesel use or electric vehicles with a commensurate growth of renewable energy sources in the grid would lower the overall GHG footprints modeled here; however, the modeling results indicate that transportation is a relatively small portion of the GHG emissions associated with organic waste management.

As SSO collections are expanded to capture a larger percentage of the organics portion of the MSW stream in the future, higher levels of physical contamination are possible (Levis et al., 2010 ). Depackaging is a system for removing a majority of physical contaminants from the SSO waste stream (Catalina Suarez Murcia et al., 2024 ). Electricity and fuel used during the depackaging process is responsible for only 3% of total GHG emissions on an absolute basis for Options 3, 4, and 5. The energy use associated with physical contaminant removal from composting operations is not well documented, consequently GHG costs associated with that process are not included in these calculations.

This modeling project included Scope 3 GHG accounting for the replacement of fertilizers when land applying compost or digestate (avoided emissions) and the production of polymers used in dewatering. For some GHG accounting protocols, Scope 3 emissions are not included (Shrimali, 2021 ). Figure 3 breaks down the total emissions for each SSO management option by scope.

Combustion of biomass in a waste‐to‐energy incineration facility was not one of the options that NYC DEP was interested in pursuing. However, at the time of modeling, 31% of MSW from NYC was going to incinerators. When using BEAM's default values for fluidized bed incinerators and the known solids content of the SSO, BEAM calculates significant GHG emissions, mostly attributed to nitrous oxide emissions produced when combusting nitrogenous wastes (BEAM default values are calculated from Suzuki et al., 2003 ). The EPA's WARM, on the other hand, estimates a net negative GHG footprint largely due to the electricity generated from combusting food waste. WARM assumes 27.8% solids for food waste (unlike in BEAM, the user cannot change this value in WARM), which provides a more favorable balance of British thermal unit value and loss of energy from evaporating water in the SSO during combustion as compared to the 11.2% solids of the SSO modeled in this study. As described by Chen et al. ( 2022 ), moisture and VS content of the material being incinerated have a significant impact on the GHG footprint of incineration, and there are still areas of uncertainty in modeling emissions associated with incineration. For the purposes of this assessment, combustion of SSO (relevant to Option 1) was assumed to be net zero; the GHG benefits of energy captured at the incinerators were assumed to be equal to the GHG debits (nitrous oxide emissions and natural gas use in the combustion process) during combustion of the SSO.

For Option 1 ‐ disposing SSO in a landfill with an aggressive methane capture strategy significantly reduces GHG emissions. Conversely, because methane is the largest contributor to the GHG footprint in this option, when looking at emissions for this option using IPCC AR6 20‐year GWPs (78 and 273 for methane and nitrous oxide, respectively), the GHG footprint more than doubles.

For Option 2 (direct‐to‐compost), using the lower carbon sequestration factor, as opposed to the food waste composting carbon sequestration factor from WARM, emissions associated with composting slightly outweigh benefits associated with carbon sequestration and fertilizer replacement. With this lower carbon sequestration factor, Option 3 is more favorable than Option 2. When modeling nitrous oxide emissions during composting, the GHG footprint increases from −0.55 to −0.4 CO 2 eq/Dry Mg SSO. Additionally, because there are some methane emissions associated with the biological process of composting, when using the 20‐year GWPs the GHG footprint of Option 2 increases but remains carbon‐negative.

For Option 3 – anaerobic digestion to disposal, flaring the biogas instead of cleaning the biogas and injecting RNG into the natural gas pipeline eliminates the renewable energy benefits to the GHG footprint and, consequently, increases overall GHG emissions for this management strategy. As with Option 1, using the 20‐year GWPs significantly increases the GHG footprint, partly due to fugitive methane emitted during flaring of biogas.

For Options 4 and 5 (anaerobically digesting the SSO followed by land application or composting), most of the sensitivity adjustments have minimal impact on GHG emissions. However, when flaring the biogas instead of injecting RNG into the pipeline, both of these options become slightly carbon‐positive. And when modeling nitrous oxide emissions from composting, the GHG footprint of Option 5 changes from −0.59 to −0.44 CO 2 eq/Dry Mg SSO.

The results from both the primary analysis and the sensitivity analyses make it clear that, unless biogas is flared instead of used for RNG, Options 4 and 5 (anaerobic digestion followed by land application or composting then land application, respectively, of the dewatered digestate) offer the most favorable GHG outcome.

The favorability of Option 2, direct‐to‐compost, including land application of the compost, is highly dependent on the carbon sequestration factor, more so than for Options 4 (anaerobic digestion to land‐application) and 5 (anaerobic digestion to compost), where the benefits of RNG to pipeline persist regardless of the carbon sequestration factor. The permanence of soil carbon introduced by organic soil amendments is both difficult to measure and highly variable. There is currently little consensus on what value to use, with published estimates ranging from 0.013 MgCO 2 eq/dry Mg biomass (Villa & Ryals, 2021 ) to 0.98 MgCO 2 eq/dry Mg biomass (EPA, 2023a ) and an array of values in between (e.g., Coleman & Jenkinson, 1996 ; Levavasseur et al., 2020 ; Parton et al., 1993 ). This highlights a need for further research on long‐term soil carbon storage and the development of a standardized framework for soil organic carbon measurement and monitoring (Lawrence et al., 2023 ).

Option 3 (anaerobic digestion to disposal) still provides for a low GHG footprint, though significantly less favorable than Options 2, 4, and 5. The exceptions are if modeled with 20‐year GWPs or if biogas is flared instead of used for RNG; in these cases, the GHG footprint is net positive.

Option 1 (disposal) remains the least favorable option in all sensitivity analyses. However, for any waste that is landfilled, this modeling effort indicates that municipalities focused on reducing emissions should focus on selecting landfills with aggressive capping and gas capture strategies is an option for reducing emissions.

When comparing the management options of diverting SSO directly to composting versus diverting the material to anaerobic digestion followed by land application or composting, there are material management considerations to consider. The SSO collected at the NYC transfer station has a low solids content, partly due to blending commercial organic waste streams with food waste streams. With the physical contamination that is expected with large‐scale SSO diversion programs (Thakali et al., 2022 ), the use of depackaging equipment to remove physical contamination results in a slurry; this high‐moisture slurry would likely be problematic for composting. With a diverse recycling program in the future, NYC may find that some SSO feedstocks are more suitable for anaerobic digestion, while some less physically contaminated, higher solids SSO may be better suited to going directly to composting.

In weighing Option 4 versus Option 5, the two options with the most similar and most favorable GHG outcomes, there are two important considerations. First is that compost is a more versatile soil amendment than dewatered digestate. Compost may be used in landscaping, gardens, and agricultural fields, whereas dewatered digestate is a moist, sometimes odoriferous material that often contains more nitrogen than compost (on a mass basis) and is best suited for use in agricultural fields rather than landscaping and gardens. Second is that composting and then land‐applying the dewatered digestate is a more labor‐intensive and costly process than simply land‐applying the dewatered digestate. In either case, NYC would likely be exporting the material to a third party to handle composting and/or land application.

Lastly, the options modeled in this GHG assessment are based on practical options available for NYC's SSO at the time of this study. It is worth noting that there are other options for waste management, including pyrolysis and combustion of SSO and/or dewatered digestate, that were not modeled in this study and may be worth considering for other waste management entities (e.g., Havukainen et al., 2022 ).

Although there is no exact comparison to this analysis in the literature due to the specifications of this SSO and the management options, other analyses have reported similar outcomes when comparing emissions from landfilling, anaerobic digestion, and composting of organic waste. Nordahl et al. ( 2020 ) found that landfilling organic waste had a significantly higher GHG footprint than composting or digesting, and composting and land‐applying the digestate rather than landfilling the digestate improved the GHG footprint. In a review of 19 studies on GHG emissions associated with food waste management, Bernstad Saraiva Schott et al. ( 2016 ) found that, when energy is recovered during digestion, anaerobic digestion is often preferable to composting (as well as to landfilling and incineration). These studies offer better comparisons for Options 1, 2, and 4 than for the other scenarios. In units of Mg CO 2 e per wet Mg of organic waste, the results from this study are 0.24 for Option 1 (landfill), −0.062 for Option 2 (direct to compost), and −0.065 for Option 4 (anaerobic digestion to land application). Findings from Nordahl et al. ( 2020 ), Bernstad Saraiva Schott et al. ( 2016 ), and Morris et al. ( 2013 ) for similar management scenarios range from 0.16 to 0.50 Mg CO 2 e per wet Mg of organic waste for landfilling, −0.21 to 0.14 for composting, and −0.39 to 0.027 for anaerobic digestion; these ranges encompass the results from this study.

Using BEAM, we achieved a high level of granularity specific to GHG emissions associated with current waste management data and diversion options that were available to NYC at the time of this study. The accompanying sensitivity analyses highlight the model's responsiveness to the values to which the model is most sensitive and to values that are most likely to change in the rapidly evolving field of GHG accounting. This assessment found that, of the SSO management options available to NYC, anaerobic digestion followed by land application of the digestate (composted or not) offered the most favorable GHG footprint, followed closely by composting without anaerobic digestion. The sensitivity analyses found that flaring the biogas from anaerobic digestion, instead of recycling it into RNG, increased the GHG footprint of the three anaerobic digestion options (Options 3, 4, and 5) and changed Options 4 and 5 from net‐negative to net‐positive (significantly less favorable). Similarly, using a lower carbon sequestration factor changed the GHG footprint of Option 2 (direct‐to‐compost) from net‐negative to net‐positive. In all the sensitivity analyses in this assessment, landfilling undigested SSO remained the least‐favorable option from a GHG perspective. As such, BEAM served as an evidence‐based decision‐support tool for NYC DEP while modeling the significant impact management decision alternatives can have on the emissions associated with organic waste management. Factors that are rapidly changing in today's waste management marketplace, including landfill management strategies and RNG use, can have dramatic impacts on emissions associated with organic waste management. The sensitivity analysis of the impact of the carbon sequestration factor utilized highlights the need for further research and consensus in GHG accounting methodologies with particular attention to the carbon sequestration factor used to calculate the permanence of carbon in land‐applied biomass. This modeling would not be possible in WARM, where there are limited options for customizing model inputs; WARM values that are not adjustable by the user include biogas collection rate, methane flare rate, fugitive emissions from digesters, solids content of organic wastes, and composting parameters such as presence of a biofilter and rate of nitrous oxide emissions. WARM also does not allow for the combination of processing options, such as digestion followed by composting or land application. Working with BEAM was essential to customizing the modeling to NYC's operations and to understanding the impact of potential management changes. Projecting increased diversion of SSO, the NYC DEP plans to expand SSO collections directed to anaerobic digestion to approximately 300,000 Mg/year by 2035. (A. Bianco, NYC DEP, personal communication, December 30, 2025). Based on the estimates from this modeling, if this material were to be managed in accordance with Option 5, the city would reduce GHG emissions by 102,005 Mg CO 2 eq/year compared to not separating that organic waste from the MSW stream.
